source.text: וַ֭יַּעַן בִּלְדַּ֥ד הַשֻּׁחִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Bildad the Shuhite and said:

en.L: And Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:
en.B: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
en.R: Then Bildad the Shuhite said:

decisions.choice: Bildad's second speech
decisions.reason: This is Bildad's second speech (chapter 18), his reply to Job's words in chapters 16-17. As at 8:1, the words that introduce a speech are prose; the speech itself is poetry.

decisions.choice: the Shuhite: from Shuah
decisions.reason: Bildad comes from Shuah, perhaps the people descended from Shuah, a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2), who lived to the east.

decisions.choice: answered (Balanced), said (Readable), without "and said"
decisions.reason: Hebrew introduces speech with two verbs, "answered and said". Literal keeps both; Balanced and Readable say it once, with the same wording at every speech introduction in Job.

source.text: עַד־אָ֤נָה׀תְּשִׂימ֣וּן קִנְצֵ֣י לְמִלִּ֑ין תָּ֝בִ֗ינוּ וְאַחַ֥ר נְדַבֵּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Until when will you set ends to words? Consider, and after we will speak.

en.L: Until when will you set ends to words? \q Consider, and afterward we will speak.
en.B: How long before you all put an end to words? \q Think it through, and then we can talk.
en.R: When will you stop making these speeches? \q Be sensible, and then we can talk.

decisions.choice: ends to words: an end to talking
alternatives: snares for words: hunting for words to trap others
decisions.reason: The word (qinze) is found only here. It is most likely a form of the word for "end" ("how long until you put an end to words?"). Others take it from a word for "snare": how long will you hunt for words to trap others? Either way Bildad is tired of Job's speeches.

decisions.choice: you (plural)
decisions.reason: The verbs are plural, though Bildad is answering Job. He may be speaking to Job together with those who think like him, or using the plural for Job as one of a kind of person; in verse 4 he turns to Job with a singular.

decisions.choice: consider: understand, think it through
decisions.reason: The verb (bin) means to understand or pay attention. Bildad says a real conversation can only begin when Job listens.

decisions.choice: you all
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that the "you" is plural (m2).

source.text: מַ֭דּוּעַ נֶחְשַׁ֣בְנוּ כַבְּהֵמָ֑ה נִ֝טְמִ֗ינוּ בְּעֵינֵיכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Why are we counted like cattle, are we stupid in your eyes?

en.L: Why are we counted as cattle, \q stupid in your eyes?
en.B: Why are we regarded as cattle, \q as stupid in your sight?
en.R: Why do you think we are as dumb as animals? \q Why do you treat us like fools?

decisions.choice: as cattle: answering Job's taunt
decisions.reason: Job told the friends to ask the beasts and the birds, since even they know what the friends claim to teach (12:7-9). Bildad takes it as an insult, as if Job had called them dumb animals.

decisions.choice: stupid: stopped up, without understanding
decisions.reason: The verb is rare. It is most likely from a root meaning to be dull or stopped up ("stupid"); some take it as "unclean". "Stupid" matches "cattle" in the first line.

decisions.choice: your: plural
decisions.reason: The "your" is plural, like the verbs of verse 2.

source.text: טֹֽרֵ֥ף נַפְשׁ֗וֹ בְּאַ֫פּ֥וֹ הַ֭לְמַעַנְךָ תֵּעָ֣זַב אָ֑רֶץ וְיֶעְתַּק־צ֝֗וּר מִמְּקֹמֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Tearing himself in his anger, for your sake will be forsaken [the] earth, and will move a rock from its place?

en.L: [You] who tear yourself in your anger, \q for your sake will the earth be forsaken, \q or a rock be moved from its place?
en.B: You who tear yourself apart in your anger, \q should the earth be abandoned for your sake, \q or the rock be moved from its place?
en.R: You are tearing yourself apart with anger. \q Should the whole earth be emptied just for you? \q Should the rocks be moved out of their place?

decisions.choice: one who tears himself: Job, addressed directly
decisions.reason: The first line is in the third person, "one who tears himself in his anger", but it describes Job, and the next words speak to him ("for your sake").

decisions.choice: tear ... in anger: turned back on Job
decisions.reason: Job said that God had torn him in his anger (16:9). Bildad answers that it is Job who tears himself apart with his own rage.

decisions.choice: a rock moved from its place: the fixed order of the world
decisions.reason: Job said that God wears away mountains and moves rocks from their place, and so destroys human hope (14:18-19). Bildad turns it round: the order of the world, where the wicked are punished, will not change just because Job protests.

decisions.choice: you who tear yourself
decisions.reason: Every level uses "you" for the third-person description, as the second half of the verse does (m1).

source.text: גַּ֤ם א֣וֹר רְשָׁעִ֣ים יִדְעָ֑ךְ וְלֹֽא־יִ֝גַּ֗הּ שְׁבִ֣יב אִשּֽׁוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Also [the] light of [the] wicked is extinguished, and not shines the flame of his fire.

en.L: Yes, the light of the wicked is put out, \q and the flame of his fire does not shine.
en.B: Yes, the light of the wicked goes out; \q the flame of his fire does not shine.
en.R: The truth is that the light of wicked people goes out. \q The flame of their fire stops shining.

decisions.choice: light ... put out: life and prosperity come to an end
decisions.reason: A lamp or fire burning in a home was a picture of life and well-being; when it goes out, the family is finished (21:17; Proverbs 13:9; 24:20). Job used the same verb of his own days (17:1).

decisions.choice: the wicked ... his: a type of person
decisions.reason: The verse begins with "the wicked" (plural) and goes on with "he" and "his" for the rest of the poem (verses 5-21). Bildad describes the typical wicked man, and the picture is meant to fit Job.

decisions.choice: also: yes, indeed
decisions.reason: The opening word is "also" or "even", here giving emphasis to the start of the description.

decisions.choice: wicked people ... their
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the plural of the first line through the verse; Literal and Balanced follow the Hebrew's shift to "his".

source.text: א֭וֹרחָשַׁ֣ךְ בְּאָהֳל֑וֹ וְ֝נֵר֗וֹ עָלָ֥יו יִדְעָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] light grows dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out.

en.L: The light grows dark in his tent, \q and his lamp above him is put out.
en.B: The light in his tent grows dark, \q and the lamp above him goes out.
en.R: The light in his home grows dark. \q The lamp over him goes out.

decisions.choice: the lamp above him: the lamp hanging in the tent
decisions.reason: A lamp hung from the roof or stood on a stand, lighting the home; its going out pictures the end of the household (verse 5).

decisions.choice: tent: home, household
decisions.reason: "Tent" is the ordinary word for a home in this poetry (5:24; 8:22; 18:14-15), whether or not one lived in a tent.

decisions.choice: home
decisions.reason: Readable says "home" for the tent (m2).

source.text: יֵֽ֭צְרוּ צַעֲדֵ֣י אוֹנ֑וֹ וְֽתַשְׁלִיכֵ֥הוּ עֲצָתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Are hemmed in the steps of his strength, and casts him down his own counsel.

en.L: The steps of his strength are hemmed in, \q and his own counsel throws him down.
en.B: His strong stride is cut short, \q and his own schemes bring him down.
en.R: He used to walk with strong steps, but now he stumbles along. \q His own plans make him fall.

decisions.choice: the steps of his strength are hemmed in: his strong stride is cut short
decisions.reason: Strong steps have room to move freely (Proverbs 4:12). Now his way is narrowed, so he can no longer walk with confidence.

decisions.choice: counsel: his own plans or schemes
decisions.reason: The word ('etsah) means advice or plan. The wicked man is brought down by his own schemes (5:13).

decisions.choice: He used to walk with strong steps, but now he stumbles along
alternatives: The steps of his strength are hemmed in
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture (m1).

source.text: כִּֽי־שֻׁלַּ֣ח בְּרֶ֣שֶׁת בְּרַגְלָ֑יו וְעַל־שְׂ֝בָכָ֗ה יִתְהַלָּֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: For he is sent into a net by his feet, and on a lattice he walks about.

en.L: For he is thrown into a net by his own feet, \q and he walks about on a lattice.
en.B: For his own feet lead him into a net, \q and he wanders onto a covered pit.
en.R: He walks right into a net. \q He steps onto a trap that is covered over.

decisions.choice: net, lattice: hunters' traps
decisions.reason: Verses 8-10 use six different words for hunters' nets and traps. The "lattice" is a mesh laid over a pit to hide it, so that an animal walking on it falls in.

decisions.choice: by his own feet: he walks into it himself
decisions.reason: No one pushes him; his own feet take him into the net, as his own schemes bring him down (verse 7).

decisions.choice: a covered pit
decisions.reason: Balanced says what the lattice is for (m1).

source.text: יֹאחֵ֣ז בְּעָקֵ֣ב פָּ֑ח יַחֲזֵ֖ק עָלָ֣יו צַמִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Takes hold on [the] heel a trap; holds fast on him a snare.

en.L: A trap seizes [him] by the heel; \q a snare holds fast on him.
en.B: A trap grabs him by the heel; \q a snare holds him tight.
en.R: A trap catches him by the heel. \q A snare holds him tight.

decisions.choice: trap, snare: devices that catch and hold an animal
decisions.reason: The trap (pach) is a bird trap or spring trap (Psalm 124:7); the second word (tsammim) is a snare that closes on its prey. The point is that he cannot escape.

decisions.choice: holds fast: grips tightly
decisions.reason: The verb (chazaq) means to be strong or to grip firmly.

source.text: טָמ֣וּן בָּאָ֣רֶץ חַבְל֑וֹ וּ֝מַלְכֻּדְתּ֗וֹ עֲלֵ֣י נָתִֽיב׃

records.literal_gloss: Hidden in the ground [is] his rope, and his trap on [the] path.

en.L: Hidden in the ground [is] a rope for him, \q and a trap for him on the path.
en.B: A noose is hidden for him on the ground, \q a trap lies in his path.
en.R: A rope is hidden on the ground to catch him. \q A trap is waiting on his path.

decisions.choice: his rope, his trap: set for him
decisions.reason: "His rope" and "his trap" are the ones meant to catch him, not ones he owns.

decisions.choice: rope: a noose or cord
decisions.reason: The word (chevel) is a cord or rope; laid on the ground, it is a noose for catching an animal by the foot.

decisions.choice: for him, in his path
decisions.reason: English "his rope" would suggest he owns it, so the levels say "for him" (m1).

source.text: סָ֭בִיב בִּֽעֲתֻ֣הוּ בַלָּה֑וֹת וֶהֱפִיצֻ֥הוּ לְרַגְלָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: All around terrify him terrors, and they scatter him at his feet.

en.L: All around, terrors frighten him, \q and they chase him at his heels.
en.B: Terrors frighten him on every side \q and dog his every step.
en.R: Terrible things frighten him on every side. \q They chase him wherever he goes.

decisions.choice: terrors: sudden horrors
decisions.reason: The word (ballahot) means sudden terror or dreadful things. It returns in verse 14, "the king of terrors".

decisions.choice: scatter him at his feet: chase him step by step
alternatives: make him run here and there
decisions.reason: The verb means to scatter or drive about. "At his feet" means close behind, at his heels: the terrors follow him wherever he goes and give him no rest.

decisions.choice: dog his every step
decisions.reason: Balanced uses an English idiom for being followed closely (m2).

source.text: יְהִי־רָעֵ֥ב אֹנ֑וֹ וְ֝אֵ֗יד נָכ֥וֹן לְצַלְעֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Is hungry his strength, and disaster [is] ready for his stumbling.

en.L: His strength is hungry, \q and disaster is ready for his stumbling.
en.B: His strength is starved, \q and disaster stands ready for him to stumble.
en.R: He grows weak with hunger, \q and disaster is ready to strike when he falls.

decisions.choice: his strength
decisions.reason: The word ('on) means strength or vigor, often the strength of manhood (verse 7; Genesis 49:3). His strength wastes away from hunger.

decisions.choice: for his stumbling: waiting for him to fall
decisions.reason: The word (tsela') means stumbling or limping (Psalm 35:15; 38:18). Disaster waits for him to slip. A word spelled the same means "side", so it may also mean that disaster stands at his side.

decisions.choice: is hungry: a statement
alternatives: let his strength be hungry: a wish
decisions.reason: The verb form can be read as a statement or a wish. In a poem describing what happens to the wicked, a statement fits best.

source.text: יֹ֭אכַל בַּדֵּ֣י עוֹר֑וֹ יֹאכַ֥ל בַּ֝דָּ֗יו בְּכ֣וֹר מָֽוֶת׃

records.literal_gloss: It eats the parts of his skin; eats his parts the firstborn of death.

en.L: It devours the parts of his skin; \q the firstborn of death devours his limbs.
en.B: Disease eats away his skin; \q the firstborn of death devours his limbs.
en.R: A deadly disease eats away his skin. \q Death's oldest son eats up his arms and legs.

decisions.choice: the firstborn of death: a deadly disease
decisions.reason: Death is pictured as a father, and his firstborn, his strongest son, is the worst of his powers, most likely a wasting disease. The first line has the same verb without a subject; the firstborn of death is the one who eats in both lines.

decisions.choice: parts: limbs
decisions.reason: The word (bad) means a part or a pole; for the body it means the limbs. It is the same word as "bars" in 17:16.

decisions.choice: his skin: what is happening to Job
decisions.reason: Job's skin is covered with sores and breaking down (2:7; 7:5; 19:20). Bildad's picture of the wicked man's sickness is aimed at Job.

decisions.choice: Disease (B), A deadly disease (R)
decisions.reason: The first line has no subject; Balanced and Readable supply what is meant (m1).

source.text: יִנָּתֵ֣ק מֵ֭אָהֳלוֹ מִבְטַח֑וֹ וְ֝תַצְעִדֵ֗הוּ לְמֶ֣לֶךְ בַּלָּהֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: He is torn from his tent, his confidence, and it marches him to [the] king of terrors.

en.L: He is torn from his tent, his confidence, \q and it marches him to the king of terrors.
en.B: He is torn from the tent where he felt safe \q and marched off to the king of terrors.
en.R: He is dragged away from the home where he felt safe. \q He is led away to death, the king of terrors.

decisions.choice: his confidence: the home he trusted in
decisions.reason: The tent is called "his confidence", the thing he trusted to keep him safe (8:14).

decisions.choice: the king of terrors: death, ruling the dead
decisions.reason: The terrors of verse 11 serve a king, Death, pictured as ruler of the underworld. The wicked man is marched to him like a captive.

decisions.choice: it marches him: the terrors or death drive him
decisions.reason: The verb is feminine, "it" or "she makes him march". It most likely refers to the terrors or to an unnamed power. It could also be read "you march him"; the sense is that he is taken by force.

decisions.choice: marched off (B), led away (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use a passive, since the subject is not named (m3).

decisions.choice: death,
decisions.reason: Readable names death (m2).

source.text: תִּשְׁכּ֣וֹן בְּ֭אָהֳלוֹ מִבְּלִי־ל֑וֹ יְזֹרֶ֖ה עַל־נָוֵ֣הוּ גָפְרִֽית׃

records.literal_gloss: Dwells in his tent [what is] none of his; is scattered over his home sulfur.

en.L: [What is] not his dwells in his tent; \q sulfur is scattered over his home.
en.B: Nothing of his remains in his tent; \q burning sulfur is scattered over his home.
en.R: Strangers live in his home. \q Burning sulfur is scattered over the place where he lived.

decisions.choice: what is not his: strangers, or nothing of his
alternatives: fire (with a small change to the letters)
decisions.reason: The words mean "from what is not his". They can mean that strangers live in his tent or that nothing of his is left there. Some suggest a slight change to read "fire", to match the sulfur. Either way his house passes out of his hands.

decisions.choice: sulfur scattered: a place destroyed by judgment
decisions.reason: Burning sulfur recalls the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24; Deuteronomy 29:22; Psalm 11:6). Sulfur may also have been spread to make a place barren or to purify it.

decisions.choice: Nothing of his remains (B), Strangers live (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say the same thing two ways that the words allow (m1): his house is no longer his.

source.text: מִ֭תַּחַת שָֽׁרָשָׁ֣יו יִבָ֑שׁוּ וּ֝מִמַּ֗עַל יִמַּ֥ל קְצִירֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: From beneath his roots dry up, and from above withers his branch.

en.L: From beneath his roots dry up, \q and from above his branch withers.
en.B: His roots dry up below, \q and his branches wither above.
en.R: He is like a tree whose roots dry up \q and whose branches wither.

decisions.choice: roots and branch: the whole man and his family
decisions.reason: He is pictured as a tree dying from root to top: nothing is left of him or his descendants (verse 19; 8:16-19; Amos 2:9; Malachi 3:19).

decisions.choice: branch: the leafy branches of a tree
decisions.reason: The word (qatsir) usually means harvest, but here and in 14:9; 29:19 it means branches.

decisions.choice: He is like a tree
decisions.reason: Readable makes the picture explicit (m1).

source.text: זִֽכְרוֹ־אָ֭בַד מִנִּי־אָ֑רֶץ וְלֹא־שֵׁ֥ם ל֝֗וֹ עַל־פְּנֵי־חֽוּץ׃

records.literal_gloss: His remembrance perishes from [the] land, and not a name [is] to him on [the] face of [the] street.

en.L: His memory perishes from the land, \q and he has no name on the face of the street.
en.B: All memory of him perishes from the land; \q no one in the street speaks his name.
en.R: People in the land forget about him. \q No one in town remembers his name.

decisions.choice: the land: the earth or the country
decisions.reason: The word ('erets) means the earth or a land. Here it is the world he lived in, where he is forgotten.

decisions.choice: name: his reputation and the memory of him
decisions.reason: To have a name is to be remembered and spoken of. The worst fate was to have one's name die out (Deuteronomy 25:6; Psalm 9:6-7; Proverbs 10:7).

decisions.choice: the street: outside, the open places
decisions.reason: The word (chuts) means outside, the street or the open country. With "land" in the first line, it may mean the countryside; with "name", the places where people meet.

source.text: יֶ֭הְדְּפֻהוּ מֵא֣וֹר אֶל־חֹ֑שֶׁךְ וּֽמִתֵּבֵ֥ל יְנִדֻּֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: They drive him from light into darkness, and from [the] world they chase him.

en.L: They drive him from light into darkness, \q and they chase him from the world.
en.B: He is driven from light into darkness \q and chased out of the world.
en.R: He is pushed out of the light into the darkness. \q He is chased out of the world.

decisions.choice: they: unnamed agents, a passive sense
decisions.reason: Hebrew often uses "they" with no subject named; the sense is passive: "he is driven", by no one in particular.

decisions.choice: from light into darkness: from life into death
decisions.reason: Light is life and darkness the world of the dead (10:21-22; 17:13).

decisions.choice: He is driven ... chased
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the passive that the unnamed "they" implies (m1).

source.text: לֹ֘א נִ֤ין ל֣וֹ וְלֹא־נֶ֣כֶד בְּעַמּ֑וֹ וְאֵ֥ין שָׂ֝רִ֗יד בִּמְגוּרָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: Not offspring to him and not descendant among his people, and none surviving in his dwellings.

en.L: He has no offspring and no descendant among his people, \q and there is no survivor where he lived.
en.B: He has no children or grandchildren among his people, \q no survivor where he once lived.
en.R: He has no children or grandchildren left among his people. \q No one in his family is left alive where he used to live.

decisions.choice: offspring and descendant: no line at all
decisions.reason: The two words (nin and neked) are a fixed pair for descendants (Genesis 21:23; Isaiah 14:22). His family line ends. For Job, whose children have died (1:18-19), this is a cruel thing to hear.

decisions.choice: dwellings: places where he stayed
decisions.reason: The word means places of sojourning, where he lived for a time.

decisions.choice: children or grandchildren
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday words for the fixed pair (m1).

source.text: עַל־י֭וֹמוֹ נָשַׁ֣מּוּ אַחֲרֹנִ֑ים וְ֝קַדְמֹנִ֗ים אָ֣חֲזוּ שָֽׂעַר׃

records.literal_gloss: At his day are appalled [those in the] west, and [those in the] east seize horror.

en.L: At his day those of the west are appalled, \q and those of the east are seized with horror.
en.B: People of the west are appalled at his fate, \q and people of the east are seized with horror.
en.R: People in the west are shocked at what happens to him. \q People in the east shudder with horror.

decisions.choice: his day: the day of his downfall
decisions.reason: "His day" is the day of his ruin (Psalm 37:13; Obadiah 12).

decisions.choice: those of the west and the east: everyone, everywhere
alternatives: those who come after and those who went before
decisions.reason: The two words mean "those behind" and "those in front". Facing east, as Hebrews did when naming directions, behind is the west and in front is the east, so the line means everyone, everywhere. The words can also mean later and earlier generations, but those who lived before him could not see his fall, so the directions fit better.

decisions.choice: his fate (B), what happens to him (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "his day" means (m1).

source.text: אַךְ־אֵ֭לֶּה מִשְׁכְּנ֣וֹת עַוָּ֑ל וְ֝זֶ֗ה מְק֣וֹם לֹא־יָדַֽע־אֵֽל׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Surely these [are the] dwellings of [the] wicked, and this [is the] place of [one who] not knew God.

en.L: Surely these [are] the dwellings of the unjust, \q and this [is] the place of [him who] did not know God.
en.B: Surely this is what becomes of the homes of the unjust, \q the place of one who does not know God.
en.R: This is what happens to the homes of evil people. \q This is what happens to someone who does not know God.

decisions.choice: the unjust: the one who does wrong
decisions.reason: The word ('avval) means an unjust or wicked person, one who does wrong to others (27:7; 29:17).

decisions.choice: one who does not know God: one who ignores God
decisions.reason: To know God is to acknowledge him and live in his ways (Jeremiah 22:16; Hosea 4:1). Bildad's closing words imply that Job is such a person.

decisions.choice: these ... this: the whole fate described
